newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dlr finds fragile rest after rowdy week.
newsitem.headline: Australian dlr finds fragile rest after rowdy week.

text.p: The Australian dollar looked to have found a short term floor Friday as a bounce from two-month lows clawed back a portion of the week's two cent loss.

The currency enjoyed a short-covering rally overnight as speculators bought in anticipation of huge U.S. coporate demand related to the imminent sale of a Victorian power station rumoured to be worth up to A$4.5 billion.

But attempts to move to safer ground foundered on the shoals of US$0.7765 resistance, with U.S. banks still inclined to sell on fears the recent dramatic contraction in the currency's yield premium over the U.S. dollar had further to run.
By 5.00 pm (0700 GMT) the local currency was relaxing at US$0.7751/56 from an early US$0.7762/67, but was still up on Thursday's late US$0.7720/25.

It was also up on the week's two-month low of US$0.7695 but far beneath last Friday's peak of US$0.7895 -- levels which analysts reckoned could constrain the currency for some time to come. Immediate guiding levels were seen at US$0.7720 and US$0.7785 and chart watchers, at least, looked for a test of the topside near term given the currency was oversold.
Dealers were more ambivalent and felt the dollar's only real hope of a rally was if the power-sale demand appeared soon.
Sources close to the deal had said details could be released as early as this weekend, but the latest rumours were the talks had hit a snag which could delay the outcome a few days.
The actual extent and timing of any A$ demand was also hard to assess -- some past bids were partly funded by debt issues here -- but the uncertainty alone should cushion the dollar.

Further out there were also expectations three Federal airports would be offloaded to consortia with large offshore interests. The potential value of these deals was harder to pin down, but rumour put it as high as A$3.0 billion.
On the crosses it was down on the week but again above lows.
The local dollar had edged up to 97.68/78 yen from a 96.50 trough offshore but was down on last Friday's 99.12/22.

It was briefly troubled by comments from Japanese Ministry of Finance forex guru Eisuke Sakakibara that the yen's weakness was not justified by fundamentals and the U.S. shared its concern over the speed of the recent fall.
The U.S. dollar also dipped in response to 125.68/73 from 125.95/00 but market expectations the Federal Reserve would hike rates next month kept a solid floor under the currency.
That prospect was not so welcome for A$ bulls since its yield premium over the U.S. currency was already under pressure.

Australian deposit rate for one year and bond yields out to two-years had already slipped below thos in the U.S. while the spread on the 10-year bond had shrunk to 94 basis points from more than 130 a few weeks ago.

And the contraction was likely to continue with domestic Q1 consumer price data next week expected to confirm the relatively subdued outlook for inflation here. In contrast, above trend growth in the U.S. could well force another Federal Reserve tightening at its May 20 meeting.
The CPI data are expected to show a modest rise of around 0.1 percent taking annual CPI growth to 1.2 from 1.5 percent.
That compares to 3.3 percent in the U.S. and if sustained whould make Australian exporters steadily more competitive vs-a-vis American companies.

The key underlying rate was seen rising around 0.3 percent so slowing annual inflation to 2.0 percent from 2.1. This would be the very bottom of the Reserve Bank's 2-3 percent target range, providing the scope for it to ease again should the real economy not show the robust recovery it expected.
As well as CPI, a long awaited ruling on a national living wage claim is due Tuesday which will have implications for monetary policy. - Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
